keyVerseText: Terrors are turned upon me: they pursue my soul as the wind: and my welfare passeth away as a cloud. my soul: Heb. my principal one
rootMeaning: The root word נָדִיב (nâdîyb) conveys the idea of being free, generous, noble, and willing-hearted. As the feminine form, נְדִיבָה (nᵉdîybâh) carries these nuances of nobility and generosity, emphasizing not just a social rank but an intrinsic quality of honor and magnanimity. This root sense enriches the English gloss by highlighting a voluntary, noble character rather than merely a title or abstract concept of soul.
usageInScripture: The word נְדִיבָה appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, translated in Job 30:15 as "my soul," reflecting a deeply personal and vital aspect of the speaker's being. The lexicon notes its plural form refers to "noble things" or noble deeds, suggesting that while its usage in Scripture is rare, it encompasses both the inner life and outward expressions of nobility. This limited but profound use shows the word can denote both the essence of life and the honorable qualities that define a person.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding נְדִיבָה as rooted in nobility and willing generosity invites believers to see their souls not merely as life forces but as dignified, precious entities created by God with an honorable purpose. This aligns with the Christian view that humans are made in God's image, called to live nobly and generously in character. The word challenges believers to cultivate a soul marked by noble deeds and a willing heart, reflecting Christ's own magnanimity. It reminds us that our spiritual identity involves both our inner being and our outward actions, united in faithfulness and honor to God.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 30:15, the phrase "they pursue my soul as the wind" uses נְדִיבָה to express the vulnerable, vital core of the speaker's existence. The term, rendered as "my principal one," underscores the preciousness and nobility of the soul being assailed by terror. This highlights the profound distress Job experiences, as his very essence—the noble, willing heart—is under relentless attack. The word deepens the emotional and spiritual weight of the verse, reminding readers of the soul's dignity even in suffering.
